summary: Defines a way for a user interface to reach a textual, DAP-like directory interface over a TCP connection. It is described as a local mechanism and is informational, not a standard.

eli5.summary: It is like a simple phone operator you can type to, who looks things up in a big directory for you.

subtitle: A simple text protocol for accessing X.500 directory services.

tldr.problem: Implementing the full X.500 Directory Access Protocol (DAP) is complex and resource-intensive, making it impractical for smaller workstations and personal computers.
tldr.mechanism: The Directory Assistance service uses a split-DUA (Directory User Agent) architecture: a capable server implements the full DAP and exposes a simpler text-based protocol to client applications over TCP/IP, separating protocol complexity from user interfaces.
tldr.outcome: This approach successfully demonstrated that directory access could be simplified for client applications without requiring each to implement the full OSI DAP protocol, enabling wider directory service adoption.

today: RFC 1202 is Informational and documents a protocol that was already in use at the time of publication. The Directory Assistance mechanism successfully addressed a practical problem in X.500 adoption, though the broader Internet eventually adopted LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, RFC 3377 and others) as the standard simplified access method for directory services.

sections.title: The Problem and Solution
sections.content:
The OSI Directory (X.500) provides a powerful infrastructure for storing and retrieving information about people and organizations. However, it is accessed through the Directory Access Protocol (DAP), which binds a Directory User Agent (DUA) client to a Directory System Agent (DSA) server. The DAP is an OSI application layer protocol that uses the rich OSI upper-layer infrastructure, but implementing it requires significant coding investment. This makes it difficult to deploy directory client applications on smaller workstations and personal computers.

The RFC details a proven mechanism that separates DAP functionality from complexity: a split-DUA model. A capable workstation or mainframe (the "Directory Assistant") implements the full DAP on behalf of client applications, exporting a simpler "Directory Assistance" (DA) protocol over standard TCP/IP connections. This allows applications to access the powerful directory infrastructure without implementing the complex DAP themselves.
sections.eli5: X.500 directories are like a huge organized library, but the instructions for using them are very complicated. This RFC creates a helper librarian who knows the complicated instructions and translates simpler requests from people.

sections.title: The Split-DUA Architecture
sections.content:
The Directory Assistance service operates with two components: a Directory Assistant server and client applications. The Directory Assistant implements two interfaces: it handles requests from clients using the simple DA protocol over TCP/IP, and it connects to the Directory System Agent (DSA) using the full DAP protocol. This architecture allows clients to benefit from directory services without implementing DAP.

The service operates using two types of TCP connections. A control connection manages the overall session between a client and the Directory Assistant; the server listens on TCP port 411. A data connection carries individual directory transactions; the server informs clients which address and port to use for data operations. This two-connection approach allows multiple directory operations to occur during a single session while maintaining clear separation between control and data.
sections.eli5: The helper librarian has a phone line (control connection) where clients can give commands, and a separate desk (data connection) where clients do actual library lookups. The helper manages both sides so the library's complicated system works with simple requests.

sections.title: The Directory Assistance Protocol
sections.content:
The Directory Assistance protocol is text-based and uses ASCII, making it simple to implement and debug. On the control connection, clients send commands like INTR (interrupt current operation), STAT (check if directory assistant is available), or QUIT (close session). Responses begin with either +OK for success or -ERR for failure.

On the data connection, clients send directory commands such as bind (connect to the directory), search (find entries), list (show children), showentry (display an entry), and others adapted from the DISH program. The directory assistant responds with different response types: numeric responses (1-5) indicate transaction status and close the connection, while letter responses (m, y, p, e, l, d, P) represent interactive operations like messages, yes/no questions, password prompts, text editing, selection lists, and name delivery.
sections.eli5: The helper librarian listens to simple commands like "search for John Smith" or "show me all entries for the US company" and converts them into complicated library instructions, then sends back the results in simple text format.

sections.title: How Clients Use the Service
sections.content:
A client application connects to the Directory Assistant on TCP port 411 and receives the address and port of the data connection endpoint. The client can then open multiple data connections for different directory operations, reusing the same control connection. For example, a client might search for a person's email address, which could involve multiple directory lookups: first searching for the person, then optionally binding to the directory with authentication, then retrieving specific attributes.

Interactive operations are supported through response mechanisms that ask clients for input, such as prompts for passwords during authentication. The response format allows for text editing when updating directory entries, and for presenting selection lists to users when a search returns multiple matches. Once a data connection operation completes, the Directory Assistant closes the data connection, but the control connection remains open for subsequent operations. This design enables persistent sessions with multiple directory lookups without repeatedly authenticating.
sections.eli5: A client calls the helper, gets sent to a desk for the actual lookup, conducts the search or edit, and when done, the desk closes but the phone line stays open so the client can make another request without calling back.
